[1;97m1.4 — the shell, caught in the act[0m

Type [92mdate[0m. Now type [92mdtae[0m.

  [92mdate[0m     [90m# prints the date and time[0m
  [92mdtae[0m     [90m# bash: dtae: command not found[0m

Read who is speaking. [92mbash:[0m is the shell. It looked for a
program called dtae, found none, and told you. When the name is
right, it finds the program and runs it; what the program prints
comes back to you.

Three parts, kept apart for the rest of this tutor:
  [36mterminal[0m  →  [36mshell[0m  →  [36mprogram[0m
The terminal is the window. The shell is the program named [92mbash[0m
that read your line. [92mdate[0m is the program it ran.

[1;97m1.5 — who else types here[0m

Everything you typed went terminal → shell → program. There is no
other way in: anything that runs a command on this machine goes
through a shell the same way.

An AI assistant that "runs commands" for you is no exception. It
types a line into a shell; the shell finds the program; the program
runs. The line it typed can be read exactly as you read your own.

So the habits in this course count twice:
  [36mread the line[0m before anyone presses Enter — you, or a helper
  [36mknow the folder[0m it will run in
  [36mread the output[0m when it comes back, instead of skimming it

[1;97mSTAGE 2 — Paths and the filesystem[0m

Four lessons, then a gate. The shell is always [36msomewhere[0m in
the filesystem; this stage teaches you to see where, look around,
move, and predict where files land.

You'll use:
  [92mpwd[0m   print where you are now
  [92mls[0m    list what's in the current folder
  [92mcd[0m    change to another folder

And the path symbols:
  [36m.[0m     this folder
  [36m..[0m    the parent folder
  [36m~[0m     your home folder

The terminal is a quiet room.
You speak to it, it answers back.
Words have shapes here, and shapes have weight.
A pipe is a doorway between rooms.

[92mcp[0m copies. The original stays.
  [92mcp hello.txt backup.txt[0m

[92mmv[0m moves. The original moves to the new name or folder.

  [92mmv hello.txt hi.txt[0m            [90m# rename[0m
  [92mmv hi.txt notes/[0m               [90m# move into a folder[0m

[92mrm[0m deletes. [91mImmediately and permanently.[0m
  [92mrm backup.txt[0m

There is no Trash and no undo. [91mLook before you press Enter —
you, or an assistant typing for you.[0m

[36mA safety habit[0m: list before you remove.
  [92mls[0m
  [92mrm <only-now-that-you-are-sure>[0m

[1;97m4.2 — the pipe[0m

A [36mpipe[0m ( [92m|[0m ) sends the standard output of one
command into the standard input of the next. [91mMost important idea
in the shell.[0m

[92mwc[0m alone counts:
  [92mwc -l poem.txt[0m          [90m# lines in poem.txt[0m

[92mwc[0m via pipe counts [36mwhatever you piped in[0m:
  [92mseq 1 100 | wc -l[0m       [90m# 100[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | wc -l[0m     [90m# how many programs are installed[0m

Pipes stack:
  [92mls /usr/bin | sort | head[0m        [90m# list → sort → first 10[0m
  [92mls /usr/bin | grep ^a[0m            [90m# names starting with 'a'[0m

  - Each piece is a normal command; only the connector is new.

[1;97m5.3 — buffer vs file[0m

This is the most important idea in this stage.

When you open a file in Vim, Vim [36mreads it into a buffer[0m —
a copy in memory. Your keystrokes change the [36mbuffer[0m, not
the file. The file on disk only changes when you [36mwrite[0m the
buffer back.

       (read)                  (edit)                     (write)

That's why Vim has separate commands for save and quit:

  [92m:w[0m    write the buffer to the file
  [92m:q[0m    quit (only if there are no unsaved changes)
  [92m:q![0m   quit and discard unsaved changes
  [92m:wq[0m   write, then quit
